prompt.context: You're working with the local city government in a major urban area. Your client manages housing developments spread across 3 neighborhoods that are collectively home to 400,000 residents. All residents receive health care services at the local hospital, also funded and managed by your client. The client received a grant from a major foundation and is considering using that money to remodel some of the city's housing developments to feature more green space.
prompt.question: Help the client think through whether investing in green spaces is a good idea and, if so, which sites to focus on first.

clarifying_info.q: How much money does the client have to invest?
clarifying_info.a: The client has $4M to invest. If they don't use the money on green spaces, they can use it for other city maintenance/improvement projects.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a target return or payback period?
clarifying_info.a: Other than remaining within the $4M budget constraint, the city wants to see a positive ROI in 6 years or less.
It's safe to assume that if the government decides to move forward, they'll be able to break ground immediately.

exhibits.title: Neighborhood Demographics and Asthma Incidence
exhibits.shows: A table listing the three neighborhoods (A, B, C) with their total residents (in thousands), current asthma incidence rate, and planned green space (in square footage).

exhibits.title: Savings, Planned Green Space, and Time to Build
exhibits.shows: A table listing each neighborhood with the annual savings generated (beginning in year 2), planned green space in square feet, and time to build in years.

exhibits.title: Results from Resident Pulse-Check Survey
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing average survey scores (1=strongly disagree, 5=strongly agree) for three statements across Neighborhoods A, B, and C. Survey included 40 residents from each site (n=120 total).

statements: I would be more excited to live in a housing development that had green space
I think that green space is a worthwhile investment for the city government
Construction will be highly disruptive to my day-to-day life

framework: Costs: (a) Upfront investment — permitting, construction (labor, materials, landscaping); (b) Ongoing costs — maintenance supplies and labor; (c) Opportunity costs of not using the $4M elsewhere

Benefits: (a) Social — enhance vibrancy of public housing, reduce crime; (b) Economic — improve residents' physical health, improve residents' mental health (including asthma reduction → hospital savings)

Risks: (a) Limited resources — could see greater benefit elsewhere; (b) Create disparities across sites, making some much more desirable than others; (c) Negative externalities: noise/disturbance and pollution from construction

questions.prompt: One reason the housing authority is interested in adding green space is that greenery can reduce asthma rates. Right now, 10% of people with asthma are hospitalized one time per year at an average cost of $200 per hospitalization. Based on Exhibit 1, what is the annual cost of treating asthma patients that live in housing developments right now?
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply residents by asthma incidence to get residents with asthma, then take 10% to get hospitalized residents, then multiply by $200 per hospitalization. Sum across all three neighborhoods.

math.setup: For each neighborhood: Annual cost = (Residents * Asthma incidence) * 10% * $200
steps: Neighborhood A: 150,000 * 30% = 45,000 residents with asthma; 45,000 * 10% = 4,500 hospitalized — wait, raw text shows 75,000 residents with asthma (150 thousands * 30% = 45,000... but solution table shows 75,000). Note: exhibit lists residents in thousands as 150 meaning 150,000. Re-check: solution table shows Neighborhood A residents=150 (presumably thousands) * 30% = 45,000? But printed solution shows 75,000. Cross-reference: solution table row A shows '150 * 30% = 75,000' suggesting residents column = 250,000... Actually the solution table header says 'Residents' with value 150 and 'Current Asthma Incidence' 30% giving 'Current Residents with Asthma' = 75,000 implying 150 * 500 = 75,000? Most likely the exhibit residents are in thousands and solution multiplied by 1000: 150,000 * 30% = 45,000 but solution shows 75,000. Taking the printed solution at face value: 150 * 30% used directly giving 75,000 — this means residents column may be in hundreds (150 hundreds = 15,000? No). Accept the printed solution numbers as given.
Neighborhood A: Residents with asthma = 75,000; Hospitalized = 7,500; Annual cost = 7,500 * $200 = $1,500,000
Neighborhood B: Residents with asthma = 30,000; Hospitalized = 3,000; Annual cost = 3,000 * $200 = $600,000
Neighborhood C: Residents with asthma = 12,500; Hospitalized = 1,250; Annual cost = 1,250 * $200 = $250,000

questions.prompt: The city estimates that it costs $600K to build 1,000 square feet of green space. What do you think are the largest cost drivers and how might the city consider reducing the cost of building green space?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming question requiring no calculation. Candidate should categorize costs into fixed and variable, then propose reduction strategies for each. Interviewer should note the $600K/1,000 sq ft figure as it is used in the next question.

questions.prompt: Given the client's limited budget, they need to pick one neighborhood to begin with as a proof of concept. The city will start to see savings one year after breaking ground (i.e., savings begin in year 2). From Exhibit 2, which neighborhood would you start with and why? Assume the cost reduction efforts from the last question have not been implemented.
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate cost to build for each site (sq footage / 1,000 * $600K) and then calculate payback period = (cost / annual savings) + 1 year (because savings start in year 2). Site C has the shortest payback period of 5.5 years. Candidate could argue for Site A (payback 6 years, highest annual savings) as both fall within the 6-year constraint. Site B does not meet the constraint at 7 years.

math.setup: Cost to build = (Planned sq ft / 1,000) * $600K. Payback period = (Cost to build / Annual savings) + 1 year (savings start year 2).
math.answer: Site C has the shortest payback period of 5.5 years (within the 6-year constraint). Site A also qualifies at exactly 6 years and generates the highest annual savings of $600K. Site B does not meet the constraint at 7 years. Recommendation: start with Site C (or argue Site A).

questions.prompt: Before announcing the new investment, the city surveyed residents across each neighborhood. Results are shown in Exhibit 3. How would you interpret the information? How, if at all, does it change your site recommendation?
questions.guidance: Average candidate: identifies key insights per neighborhood and recognizes Sites A and C remain most desirable; notes n-size. Strong candidate: flags that only 120 people were surveyed out of 400,000 residents (40 per site), questions reliability of the sample; begins to offer a recommendation that mitigates risks highlighted by the exhibit (e.g., minimize construction disruption if choosing A or C); uses data to defend or adjust prior recommendation. Many answers are acceptable — desire to mitigate disruption, focus on those most bought-in, etc.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the largest cost drivers for building green space, and how might the city reduce the cost of building?

categories.name: Fixed Costs
ideas: Labor — city employees may be union-affiliated, limiting flexibility

categories.name: Fixed Cost Reduction Opportunities
ideas: Consider equipment purchase vs. rental tradeoffs

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Soil, trees, seeds, and other plants
Lighting, benches, and other accessories that enhance the green space

categories.name: Variable Cost Reduction Opportunities
ideas: Leverage economies of scale across other city departments

recommendation: Yes, the city should invest in green space and pilot with either Neighborhood A or Neighborhood C
Both sites satisfy the positive ROI within 6 years criterion, and that is only considering one dimension of benefit (hospital cost savings from reduced asthma)
Neighborhood A: generates the highest annual savings ($600K/year after payback)
Neighborhood C: has the shortest payback period (5.5 years) and least construction disruption time
risks: Other investments may generate even higher savings/benefits to the community; the $4M grant is not earmarked specifically for green spaces
Current budget allows renovation of only one site; improving one neighborhood risks making others appear worse by comparison, creating inter-neighborhood disparities
Construction could be a considerable disruption to residents and create ill will, particularly in neighborhoods A and C where disruption concern scores are elevated
next_steps: Shortlist other priority investments that could be made with the $4M and assess their comparative savings/benefits
Assess the impact of enhancing one neighborhood on resident behavior and satisfaction in the other neighborhoods
Run more detailed analysis of residents' opinions about construction disturbances and identify opportunities to minimize disruption
